<!-- section:hearth-m02-l01-understand -->

Bakers express every ingredient as a percentage of the flour weight. Water divided by flour is the hydration. A dough with 500 g of flour and 350 g of water is at 70% hydration.

Hydration predicts handling. At 65% a dough holds its shape readily; at 80% it spreads unless you build strength with folds and careful shaping. Starter adds both flour and water, so include its share when you want the true figure.

<!-- section:hearth-m02-l01-example -->

A fictional recipe lists 450 g flour, 330 g water and 100 g starter at 100% hydration (50 g flour and 50 g water). Total flour is 500 g and total water 380 g, so the dough is at 76% hydration, not the 73% the flour and water lines alone suggest.

At 76% the baker plans four sets of folds and a firm pre-shape, because the dough will relax more than a 65% loaf.

<!-- section:hearth-m02-l01-exercise -->

A dough uses 800 g flour, 600 g water and 160 g starter at 100% hydration. Calculate the true hydration and say how you would adjust the folding plan compared with a 68% dough.

<!-- section:hearth-m02-l01-solution -->

Total flour is 880 g and total water 680 g, so hydration is 680 / 880, about 77%. That is noticeably slacker than 68%, so add folds, handle with wet hands and give the pre-shape a longer rest before final shaping.

<!-- section:hearth-m02-l01-revisit -->

Revisit this lesson when a dough behaves differently from its recipe: recompute the hydration including the starter before changing anything else.
